title: Muscles of mastication & facial expression
blurb: The four chewing muscles, the muscles that move the face, and the nerves that drive each group.
question: The day after a lower wisdom tooth was removed under an inferior dental block, a patient rings to say they can only open their mouth a finger's width and the side of their face feels stiff. Which muscles are involved, and why might this happen after an IDB?

teach.body: The muscles you meet in dentistry fall into two groups. The muscles of mastication move the mandible to bite and chew. There are four pairs, and all are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V). The muscles of facial expression move the lips, cheeks, eyelids and forehead. They are supplied by the facial nerve (VII). Learning which nerve drives which group explains a lot of what you see chairside.

teach.body: Masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid all elevate the mandible: they close the mouth and give biting force. Lateral pterygoid is the odd one out. It pulls the condyle and disc forward, which protrudes the jaw and starts the mouth opening. When the left and right lateral pterygoids work alternately, the jaw swings from side to side to grind food. Opening is helped by the muscles under the chin (the suprahyoid muscles, such as digastric and mylohyoid) and by gravity.

These muscles lie just under the skin. Orbicularis oris encircles the mouth and closes the lips. Buccinator forms the cheek: it presses food back onto the teeth while you chew and keeps the cheek out of the way. Mentalis raises the chin and lower lip, and zygomaticus major pulls the corners of the mouth up in a smile. Lip and cheek muscles push against dentures, so the dentist moulds impressions to their movement for a stable fit.

Trismus is difficulty opening the mouth caused by spasm of the muscles of mastication. It can follow an IDB (the needle passes through or near the medial pterygoid), a difficult lower third molar extraction, or infection such as pericoronitis. Weakness of the facial muscles points to the facial nerve: in Bell's palsy, or if local anaesthetic reaches the facial nerve in the parotid gland, one side of the face droops and the eye may not close, so the eye must be protected until it recovers.

teach.text: Lateral pterygoid is the ONLY muscle of mastication that opens the mouth. And buccinator is NOT a muscle of mastication, even though it helps chewing: it is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the facial nerve.

items: Mastication: masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid; all supplied by V3.
Masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid close the jaw; lateral pterygoid opens and protrudes it.
Facial expression: orbicularis oris, buccinator, mentalis, zygomaticus and others; all supplied by the facial nerve (VII).
Trismus = spasm of the chewing muscles; facial droop = a facial nerve problem.

summary: You can now name the four muscles of mastication, say where each runs and what it does, explain which close and which opens the jaw, name the key muscles of facial expression, and link trismus and facial weakness to the trigeminal and facial nerves.

A.q: Which muscle of mastication helps to open the mouth?
A.why: Lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle and disc forward, protruding the jaw and starting the opening movement.

whyNot.0: Masseter is the strongest closing muscle.
whyNot.1: Medial pterygoid closes the jaw and helps side-to-side movement.
whyNot.2: Temporalis closes the jaw; its back fibres pull it backwards.

A.q: Which nerve supplies the muscles of mastication?
options: The mandibular division of the trigeminal
The maxillary division of the trigeminal
A.why: All four muscles of mastication are supplied by motor branches of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve.

whyNot.0: The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression.
whyNot.2: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the muscles of the tongue.
whyNot.3: The maxillary division is sensory only and carries no motor fibres.

A.q: While chewing, a patient keeps biting their cheek. Which muscle normally keeps the cheek clear and pushes food back onto the teeth?
A.why: Buccinator forms the cheek and presses food back onto the biting surfaces during chewing.

whyNot.1: Masseter closes the jaw; it lies outside the cheek and does not control it.
whyNot.2: Mentalis raises the chin and lower lip.
whyNot.3: Medial pterygoid closes the jaw from the inner side of the ramus.

B.q: A patient is asked to clench their teeth and the dentist feels a muscle bulge over the angle of the jaw. Which muscle is it?
B.why: Masseter runs from the zygomatic arch to the outer ramus and angle and bulges visibly when you clench.

whyNot.0: Temporalis can be felt at the temple, not over the angle.
whyNot.1: Buccinator is the thin cheek muscle and doesn't bulge on clenching.

B.q: Where does temporalis insert on the mandible?
options: The inner surface of the angle
B.why: Temporalis passes under the zygomatic arch and inserts on the coronoid process and front of the ramus.

whyNot.0: The condyle neck is where lateral pterygoid inserts.
whyNot.2: The inner angle is where medial pterygoid inserts.
whyNot.3: The genial tubercles anchor tongue and floor-of-mouth muscles.

B.q: Which of these is NOT a muscle of mastication?
B.why: Orbicularis oris closes the lips; it is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the facial nerve.

whyNot.0: Medial pterygoid is one of the four muscles of mastication.
whyNot.1: Temporalis is one of the four muscles of mastication.
whyNot.2: Lateral pterygoid is one of the four muscles of mastication.

C.q: After an IDB, a patient's eye on the same side will not close and the corner of the mouth droops. Which nerve has been affected?
C.why: If anaesthetic reaches the facial nerve in the parotid gland, the muscles of facial expression on that side are temporarily paralysed.

whyNot.1: The lingual nerve is sensory to the tongue; it doesn't move facial muscles.
whyNot.2: The long buccal nerve is sensory to the cheek and buccal gum.
whyNot.3: The inferior alveolar nerve is sensory to the lower teeth and lip; numbness is expected, not droop.

options: Grinding of the teeth at night
Loss of feeling in the lower lip
C.why: Trismus is restricted mouth opening caused by spasm of the muscles of mastication.

whyNot.1: Clicking is a sign of a TMJ disorder, not trismus.
whyNot.3: Lip numbness is altered sensation from the inferior alveolar or mental nerve.

C.q: Which two muscles form a sling around the angle of the mandible?
C.why: Masseter attaches to the outer angle and medial pterygoid to the inner angle, cradling it between them.

whyNot.0: Temporalis attaches to the coronoid process, and buccinator is a cheek muscle.
whyNot.2: Lateral pterygoid attaches to the condyle neck, and mentalis to the chin.
whyNot.3: Lateral pterygoid attaches near the joint, not around the angle.

reteach.title: Feel the muscles on your own face
reteach.question: You can find three of the four chewing muscles with your own fingertips. Try it as you read.

blocks.body: Put your fingers on your temples and clench: the muscle that tightens is temporalis. Move your fingers down to the angle of the jaw and clench again: the thick muscle that bulges is masseter. Now put a fingertip just in front of your ear and open wide: you feel the condyle slide forward, pulled by lateral pterygoid, which is too deep to touch. Medial pterygoid is hidden inside the ramus. Finally, puff out your cheeks and purse your lips: that is buccinator and orbicularis oris, worked by a different nerve.

explain.body: Masseter (zygomatic arch to outer angle), temporalis (side of skull to coronoid process) and medial pterygoid (pterygoid plate to inner angle) all lift the mandible to close the mouth and bite.

items.label: strongest closer; bulges when you clench
fan-shaped at the temple; inserts on the coronoid

test.q: Which muscle runs from the zygomatic arch to the outer surface of the ramus?
test.why: Masseter arises from the zygomatic arch and inserts on the outer surface of the ramus and angle.

whyNot.0: Temporalis arises from the side of the skull and inserts on the coronoid process.
whyNot.1: Medial pterygoid inserts on the inner surface of the ramus.
whyNot.3: Lateral pterygoid inserts on the condyle neck and disc.

explain.body: Lateral pterygoid runs forward from the condyle neck and joint disc to the pterygoid plate. It pulls the condyle forward to protrude the jaw and open the mouth; the two sides working in turn grind food side to side.

test.q: A patient pushes their lower jaw forward. Which muscles mainly produce this movement?
test.why: Both lateral pterygoids contracting together pull the condyles forward, protruding the mandible.

whyNot.2: The back fibres of temporalis pull the jaw backwards, the opposite movement.
whyNot.3: Buccinators are cheek muscles and do not move the jaw.

explain.body: Thin muscles under the skin, all supplied by the facial nerve. Orbicularis oris closes the lips, buccinator holds the cheek against the teeth, mentalis raises the lower lip and chin. They affect denture stability and are paralysed on one side in Bell's palsy.

test.q: Which nerve supplies orbicularis oris and buccinator?
test.why: All muscles of facial expression, including orbicularis oris and buccinator, are supplied by the facial nerve (VII).

whyNot.0: The trigeminal supplies the muscles of mastication and sensation to the face.
whyNot.1: The glossopharyngeal nerve serves the back of the tongue and throat.
whyNot.2: The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue.

explain.body: Spasm of the muscles of mastication, so the mouth will not open fully. Causes include an IDB needle passing through medial pterygoid, difficult lower third molar surgery and infection such as pericoronitis. Report it to the dentist.

steps.label: Limited opening
steps.sub: Patient reports a stiff, tight jaw

test.q: Which is a recognised cause of trismus after dental treatment?
test.why: The IDB needle passes through or near medial pterygoid, and bleeding or irritation there can cause muscle spasm.

whyNot.1: Fluoride varnish is painted on the teeth and does not affect the chewing muscles.
whyNot.2: A routine scale and polish is not a recognised cause of trismus.
whyNot.3: An alginate impression is quick and does not injure the muscles.
